title: Critical-Error Benchmark for Legal Transcription AI
one_liner: An independent, reporter-built test suite that scores transcription AI on the errors that lose cases, such as dropped negatives, swapped numbers, wrong speaker and uh-huh versus huh-uh. Court and law-firm buyers pay for procurement reports, and vendors pay for certification.
customer: State court administrative offices and county courts running digital-recording or AI pilots. Large law firm innovation and procurement teams. Insurer litigation-management groups. The AI transcription vendors themselves, who buy a certification badge.
problem: Every vendor claims 95-99% accuracy, measured as word error rate on clean audio. That metric treats 'I did not see him' becoming 'I did see him' as one wrong word in six, no worse than a dropped 'the.' Reporters know the real failure points: negations, numbers (fifteen versus fifty), proper names, speaker attribution in crosstalk, uh-huh versus huh-uh, soft-spoken witnesses, and interpreted testimony. Court procurement officers and firm buyers have no independent comparison, so RFPs copy vendor claims.
solution: Build a hidden test set from staged mock depositions and hearings. Working reporters play scripted witnesses and attorneys, recorded in courtroom reverb, on Zoom, with masks, accents and interpreters. Each recording has certified steno ground truth and annotated critical-error spans. Publish a Critical Error Rate per hour with per-category scores. Release a free public subset and leaderboard for credibility. Charge for private bake-offs on a buyer's own audio, graded by reporters. Sell annual certification with re-testing whenever a vendor updates its model.
why_now: Shortages are pushing courts to adopt digital and AI reporting, and Texas, North Dakota and California have all moved on it in different ways. The federal proposal for new Rule 707 signals that courts want reliability standards for machine output. Vendors are consolidating (Verbit owns Veritext). State court technology offices are writing RFPs now with no independent yardstick.
revenue_model: $15,000-$40,000 per court or firm procurement evaluation. $25,000-$75,000 per year per vendor for certification and re-testing. $3,000-$8,000 per year for benchmark subscription reports to firms and insurers. Licensing test sets to vendors under strict separation from the certification arm.
non_obvious_insight: Accuracy is measured by the people selling it. The profession that produces legal ground truth for a living is the natural auditor. A dropped 'not' is the error class that ends careers in this field, and word error rate hides it as noise.
first_30_days: Hire 8 working reporters at $75-$100 per hour for weekend sessions. Produce 20 hours of staged audio and run 6 vendors. Publish a free 'Negation Error Report' that reporter associations will share. Email 15 state court technology officers and the National Center for State Courts. Offer each vendor a free re-test to start certification conversations.

title: Layoff Early-Warning for Credit Unions
one_liner: Turns public WARN notices and layoff signals into member-level outreach lists, so lenders can offer hardship plans about 60 days before payments are missed.
customer: Credit unions (roughly 4,400 in the US), community banks, mortgage servicers and auto lenders pay $1.5-6k a month, often via credit-union service organisations.
problem: White-collar layoffs are lumpy and local (information-sector employment fell 23k in one Aug 2026 month, Amazon cut ~16,000 corporate roles). Lenders learn about them from missed payments, when charge-off risk is already high and members are hardest to help. Hardship programs exist but outreach comes too late.
solution: Ingest state WARN databases, news and layoff trackers. Match employers to the lender's book using payroll ACH descriptors on member accounts. Rank members by exposure, then supply compliant outreach scripts, pre-approved skip-a-pay or modification offers, and uplift measurement.
why_now: Layoffs are steady and concentrated in higher-balance, AI-exposed white-collar borrowers. Payroll descriptors and open-banking data make the join easy. Small lenders have no data teams, and the low-hire market makes re-employment slow (7-13 months in practitioner reports).
revenue_model: SaaS at $1.5-6k a month per institution, or a performance fee on avoided delinquencies.
non_obvious_insight: The layoffs are public. The scarce piece is the join to the lender's book via payroll descriptors. Employees of a laid-off employer often bank at the same local credit union, so the risk is concentrated, and the ROI is stated in avoided charge-offs rather than charity.
first_30_days: Normalise 50 state WARN sources. Backtest with a friendly credit union on two past layoff events to show missed payments 45-90 days later. Get two credit-union service organisations to run a paid $1k-a-month pilot.

title: Payroll and Proof-of-Trust for Household Staff
one_liner: A WhatsApp payroll, advance and verified-record product for Nigeria's drivers, housekeepers, nannies and gatemen, paid for by their employers.
customer: Middle- and upper-income households in Lagos and Abuja (Lekki, Ikoyi, VI, Ikeja GRA, Maitama) that employ domestic staff. Placement agencies as a channel. Diaspora children who pay for home-care of ageing parents.
problem: Millions of household workers are paid in cash or ad-hoc transfers, with no records, no pension, no health cover and no credit history. Employers act as lender of last resort, giving 3-5 untracked advances a year for school fees and emergencies. That breeds resentment, sudden resignations and theft accusations. Placement agencies charge roughly a month's salary and rely on 'guarantor forms' that everyone knows can be faked. Staff are excluded from credit even after 10 years of steady pay.
solution: The employer sets each worker's salary and pay date on WhatsApp and pays through the platform. The system runs an NIN/BVN check at hire, records every advance and auto-deducts repayment from next month's pay, and keeps a payslip history. The worker gets a wallet, an optional micro-pension contribution and health-cover add-on, and a payment-history record that lenders can use for the first genuine loan of their life. Agencies get a 'verified staff' badge and a share of revenue in return for onboarding their clients.
why_now: Wallet and bank-account penetration among lower-income workers is now high enough that most domestic staff already hold OPay, Moniepoint or PalmPay accounts. NIN/BVN verification APIs are cheap. Salary advances and lending are moving into the regulated FCCPC and CBN perimeter, and households are more cost-squeezed and more digital than in 2020. Voice-note and WhatsApp interfaces in English, Pidgin and Yoruba are finally reliable.
revenue_model: Employer subscription of about N2,000-3,000 per worker per month. A small fee on advances routed through employer-funded 'advance limits'. Commissions on micro-pension, health-cover and eventual worker microloans. Placement-agency referral share and verified-staff certificate fees.
non_obvious_insight: The real customer is the employer's peace of mind, not the worker's financial inclusion. Households will pay to stop the awkward informal-lender relationship and the fear of being scammed by staff with fake guarantors. The worker's payment history is a credit dataset that no bureau holds, and the employer pays to create it.
first_30_days: Ship a WhatsApp bot with a simple payslip and advance ledger, using a bank-partner payout API. Sign 8-10 placement agencies in Lekki, Ikoyi and Maitama and pilot with 100 households through their client lists and estate WhatsApp groups. Charge from day one, since these households are not price-sensitive. Use the first 300 workers' history to design a pilot micro-loan with a partner MFB.

title: Rescue Orphaned Steno Notes With Stroke-Level AI
one_liner: A translation service that turns retired or deceased reporters' unreadable steno files into certifiable transcripts for stalled appeals, using a neural stroke-to-text model in place of the missing personal dictionary.
customer: County and state court administrators, public defender and appellate defender offices, and state AG appellate divisions. Secondary customers are retiring reporters and their estates. The first buyer is an appellate defender office with transcript orders stuck because the reporter left, paying about $2.50-$4 per page with a $1,500 minimum.
problem: Steno notes are a personal code, not a shared language. Another reporter cannot read them without the writer's dictionary, which holds phonetic strokes plus thousands of private shortcuts called briefs. When a reporter retires, dies or moves away, their untranscribed notes are effectively dead. Appeals stall for months, and courts may have to redo hearings or accept an inadequate record. Retention rules (California is 10 years for criminal cases and 5 for most others) mean old notes are also being boxed up or destroyed as reporters retire. The average reporter is in their mid-50s, and the workforce has shrunk about 21% in a decade.
solution: Train a stroke-sequence model. Input is the raw stroke stream with timestamps. Output is English with punctuation and Q/A structure. Training data comes from open steno corpora and community theory dictionaries, synthetic strokes with randomized personal-brief variation, and consented archives from retired reporters. Where the reporter also ran a backup audio recording, fuse audio and strokes to resolve homophones. Sell three products. (1) Rescue: per-page conversion, human-scoped by a retired reporter who certifies the transcript as prepared from the original reporter's notes. (2) Archive escrow: retiring reporters pay a one-time fee or a small monthly fee to have notes and dictionary converted, indexed and held by a custodian that satisfies retention rules. (3) Later, a scoping copilot for active reporters, who spend 1-3 hours editing per hour of testimony.
why_now: The 2026 retirement wave is here, and NCRA-cited data puts the average member age around 56. The 5-10 year retention windows for notes written in 2016-2021 are closing now. California's 2026 Supreme Court ruling (Family Violence Appellate Project v. Superior Court) requires courts to give indigent litigants a verbatim record on request, which will create more appeals that need transcripts. Sequence models can now handle noisy phonetic-to-text conversion with context, and the open steno community (Plover) has published theory and dictionaries.
revenue_model: Per-page rescue fees, priced below the $4-6 ordinary transcript rate and paid by courts or appellate offices. Escrow and conversion packages for retirees (about $300-$800 one-time, or $25 per month). Annual contracts with court systems for backlog clearing. Later, a $99-$149 per month scoping copilot for active reporters, who already pay $3,000+ for CAT software.
non_obvious_insight: Only the writer can read steno notes. Court administrators do not track how many untranscribed notes sit with reporters about to retire. The stroke stream is also a cleaner input than audio, because a trained human already resolved the speaker, punctuation and homophones in real time. Almost nobody outside the profession knows the raw-notes problem exists.
first_30_days: Recruit 2-3 retired reporters through state association retiree lists. They donate or license old practice files and act as reviewers and certifiers. Build a baseline model on synthetic and open steno data, then test it blind on their files and record the accuracy. Cold-call 10 appellate defender and public defender offices with one question: do you have appeals stalled because the reporter is unavailable? Close 2-3 paid pilots at the $1,500 minimum.

title: Digital Legacy Setup Sold Through Wealth Advisors
one_liner: A white-labeled 'digital safety and legacy' visit for advisors' 80+ clients, paid for by the advisor as a retention and heir-acquisition tool.
customer: Independent RIAs and trust departments with $100M-$2B in assets and many clients over 78, plus elder-law attorneys as a secondary channel.
problem: Industry surveys often find that a majority of heirs fire their parents' advisor after an inheritance. Regulators also expect vigilance on senior clients, with trusted-contact requirements (FINRA 4512) and hold authority (Rule 2165). Meanwhile the 80-year-old's digital life (email, photos, passwords, crypto, cloud accounts, carrier, bank portals) is unmanaged. When they die or lose capacity the family can't get in, and scammers can.
solution: A 90-minute in-home or video visit by a trained 'digital steward': account inventory, password manager and passkey setup, Apple Legacy Contact and Google Inactive Account Manager set up, carrier port-out locks and credit freezes, bank alerts with 2FA routed to a trusted contact, and a family emergency binder handed to the heir or trustee. The heir joins the final visit, introduced by the advisor as the person who organized it. Add an annual re-check.
why_now: The multi-trillion-dollar generational wealth transfer is underway. More wealth sits in crypto and online accounts. Deepfake voice-clone scams target seniors. Apple and Google have shipped legacy-contact features but adoption is low, and FINRA's 2026 oversight report keeps trusted-contact practices in focus.
revenue_model: $450-900 per client visit paid by the advisor, who may pass it through, plus a $150/yr maintenance subscription. Referral fees from elder-law attorneys.
non_obvious_insight: The payer isn't the 80-year-old. It's the advisor, whose most valuable asset, the client relationship, is about to leave with the heirs. A digital steward visit is a useful favor that puts the advisor in the room with the next generation, and it doubles as compliance-friendly protection.
first_30_days: Recruit 5-10 RIAs through one advisor community (XYPN or local FPA chapters) and offer 3 free client visits each in exchange for feedback and a signed pilot. Hire retired IT pros or college students and train them on a checklist. Track how many heirs attend and whether advisors get follow-up meetings.

title: One-Filing Shield for At-Risk Public Servants
one_liner: A single intake that files every county office's address-confidentiality forms, fixes what gets recorded next, and monitors leaks for judges, election officials and clinicians.
customer: County and municipal risk pools and insurers, state associations of election officials, clerks, judges and school boards, hospital systems and physician groups (employer benefit), and police unions. Paid per protected person per year.
problem: A determined stalker can find almost anyone's home address in 30 seconds through deeds, the assessor roll, the voter file, court files, marriage licenses and business filings. Confidentiality and redaction laws now exist in 30+ states, but each office (recorder, assessor, treasurer, court clerk, voter registration, business filings) has its own form and process, and none talk to each other. Redaction usually masks the online index while the image stays retrievable at the counter and in bulk data purchases, so people-search brokers re-scrape it. Broker-removal services only hit the last layer. Clerks are ministerial and legally barred from advising anyone, so nobody explains the fix.
solution: A concierge plus software product. One intake produces and files every state- and county-specific confidentiality request across all relevant offices, with notary and wet-ink logistics handled. A local attorney network handles retitling into a privacy land trust or LLC with agent-signed deeds and mailing-address-only recording before anything new is recorded. It moves the voter registration to protected status, scrubs business filings, monitors new recordings and assessor changes monthly for the client's name, and runs broker takedowns as a final layer. Publish a free county-by-county confidentiality forms map as the top-of-funnel.
why_now: The June 2025 Minnesota lawmaker shootings, in which the suspect allegedly used people-search sites to compile officials' addresses, pushed a wave of new laws. California AB 302 requires deletions within five days from August 1, 2026, and Delaware, Florida and Georgia have judge-protection statutes. Threats against election officials and the November 3, 2026 midterms keep the issue hot, and insurers are pushing risk mitigation onto pools and employers.
revenue_model: $180-$450 per protected person per year as a benefit purchased by pools, associations or employers, plus a one-time onboarding fee and attorney-fulfilled trust-deed packages at cost plus margin. Group pricing for a pool covering hundreds of officials.
non_obvious_insight: Redaction in a county system is a display mask, not deletion, so the leak returns through the image and bulk data. The real protection is changing what gets recorded before it is recorded, which is precisely what a clerk cannot tell anyone. The 'first mile' data source is the county, not the broker, and nobody in the privacy-service industry works the six separate county offices.
first_30_days: Pick one state with a friendly clerks' association and do concierge onboarding at cost for about 20 county clerks and election officials through that association. Publish the county-by-county forms map to earn trust and backlinks. Pitch one county risk pool a 100-person pilot at $250 per person, line up one local attorney for the trust-deed workflow, and collect testimonials from the first cohort.

title: Certification-Ready OS for Sober Living Operators
one_liner: Software and audit-readiness for independent recovery residences, so the good operators become visible, certified and eligible for opioid-settlement and referral funding.
customer: Independent sober living and recovery residence operators (8-40 beds), who pay a monthly subscription. Counties, states and treatment programs later pay for verified-quality dashboards.
problem: Sober living is a largely informal industry with a few notorious bad actors. States are moving to certification, and funding streams increasingly require it. Good small operators run on spreadsheets and can't prove house rules, incident handling, naloxone logs, drug-testing policies and fair-housing compliance. Funders and hospital discharge planners can't tell who is real.
solution: A recovery-residence operating system built around the NARR standard and each state's certification rules. It covers rent and bed management, house-rule acknowledgments, incident and naloxone logs, drug-test policy records, complaint handling and resident outcomes. It has a gap assessment and mock certification audit, and generates an audit binder. A separate funder dashboard reports verified occupancy and quality metrics.
why_now: Ohio made certification mandatory in January 2025, and Virginia followed in July 2025. New York launched its first recovery residence certification program in early 2025. Certification has become a gatekeeper for state opioid-response subawards, opioid-settlement contracts and Medicaid reimbursement in some states. The SUPPORT reauthorization signed December 1, 2025 extended HUD's Recovery Housing Program and SAMHSA grants through FY2030.
revenue_model: $199-499 per house per month for the operating system. $1,500-3,000 certification-prep packages. Annual license fees from counties, health plans or opioid-settlement administrators for verified-bed and quality dashboards. Do not take pay-per-referral fees: federal and state patient-brokering laws (such as EKRA) make that dangerous.
non_obvious_insight: The gray market's problem is invisibility as much as bad operators: funders have no cheap way to tell good houses from bad. The trusted data trail is the product. The business model rule is to sell software to operators and dashboards to funders, and never take referral commissions. That keeps the network legally clean and trusted by courts, hospitals and families, which is what makes it hard to copy.
first_30_days: Pick one state with a new certification mandate (Ohio or Virginia). Offer 10 operators a free gap assessment against the NARR standard through state recovery-housing associations. Convert them to a $199/month readiness plan. Meet the state certifying body to align templates. Pitch one county opioid-settlement administrator on a pilot verified-bed dashboard.

title: Agent-Populated Simulated First Job for Juniors
one_liner: A 12-week simulated first job where new grads work inside a persistent fake company staffed by AI coworkers, clients and managers, producing an auditable work record employers trust.
customer: Employers pay $4-8k per hire or subscribe to pre-screened cohorts. Universities and bootcamps pay per-seat licences ($500-1,500), and state workforce boards fund seats. Start with RevOps, FP&A or customer-success analyst roles.
problem: The bottom rung is gone. Employers don't hire juniors because AI absorbs the tasks they learned on, and internships or apprenticeships need employer bandwidth, the very thing missing. Grads can't get the experience employers demand (Stanford: 19% gap, 42% underemployment).
solution: A persistent multi-agent world with a messy CRM or ledger, a ticket queue, stakeholder agents with hidden goals who change requirements, an AI manager giving 1:1s and an on-call incident. The junior works with their own AI tools and everything is logged. Senior humans grade a few deliverables weekly. The output is a portable 'experience ledger' (hours, artifacts, review outcomes, error-detection rates) employers can inspect.
why_now: Long-horizon agent capability and multi-agent simulation now make believable coworkers affordable (Project Vend-style and TheAgentCompany-style experiments), employers say they can't evaluate candidates in AI-permitted interviews, and the freeze is widening.
revenue_model: Employer per-hire success fees and pre-screen subscriptions, university licences and modest learner fees.
non_obvious_insight: The cold start of apprenticeship marketplaces is employer supply. A simulation removes it: the employer is fake but the evaluation is real. Employers hire on traces of judgment rather than resumes, and the moat is a scenario library built from anonymised real incidents.
first_30_days: Build one role sim (RevOps analyst) with 4 agent personas. Run it with 20 recent grads via a college career centre. Get 5 mid-size SaaS employers to review the graduates' traces and commit to interviews.

title: Pull-the-Plug Testing for Hospitals and Water Plants
one_liner: Bring data center-grade full-facility blackout testing to hospitals, water utilities and other critical facilities that never actually pull the plug, and help them source scarce backup gear the AI build-out has hoarded.
customer: Critical-access and rural hospitals, water and wastewater districts, 911 centers, cold-chain warehouses and municipal facilities. Secondary payers: property insurers, hospital captives and risk pools that can subsidize tests or discount premiums for certified resilience.
problem: Routine emergency-power testing is usually a short, partial-load generator run. It rarely exercises the whole chain (utility loss, ATS transfer, sequenced load pickup, cooling, fuel supply, paralleling controls) under real load, so the interaction failures show up during the actual storm or grid event. At the same time the AI build-out has swallowed generator, switchgear and transformer production, with multi-year lead times, so a failed generator or breaker at a small hospital cannot be replaced quickly. Facility managers know their fragile points but have no credible way to test them or to find spares.
solution: A one-day 'controlled blackout' service using data center IST discipline: written sequence-of-operations script, load-bank top-up to real facility load, thermographic and breaker health checks before and after, a witnessed utility-loss transfer, fuel/cooling/ventilation checks, and a punch list. Deliver a resilience certificate with prioritized fixes and remaining-life estimates. Upsell: source and retest certified pre-owned generators, ATS and switchgear from cancelled or paused data center orders, and keep a small regional spares pool for members of a hospital or water-district cooperative.
why_now: AI infrastructure is consuming electrical gear supply (transformer lead times of 3-5 years, switchgear reportedly sold out into 2028) while nearly half of planned 2026 US data center builds are delayed or canceled, which leaves stranded but scarce gear. Storm and grid-stress events are also raising the stakes for small critical facilities. Insurers are scrutinizing resilience, and rural facilities cannot afford the big-firm engineering studies.
revenue_model: $18K-45K per facility test; annual re-test contracts; 10-15% sourcing margin on certified pre-owned gear; insurer or captive partnership fees per policyholder tested; small monthly membership for spares-pool access.
non_obvious_insight: In a data center nobody trusts backup power until someone has pulled the plug at full load, and most first tests find something. The rest of critical infrastructure, which arguably matters more, almost never does this because the fear of a failed test outweighs the fear of a failed emergency. A Cx lead who has run hundreds of pull-the-plug tests can make the test routine and safe. The AI boom also turns the spare-gear problem into a secondary market that only someone who has seen the cancellations firsthand can source from.
first_30_days: Rent a 500 kW-1 MW load bank and partner with an electrical contractor. Call 10 facility directors at critical-access hospitals and rural water districts through state hospital and rural water associations. Offer 2 discounted first tests in exchange for case studies and insurer introductions. Approach one regional property insurer or hospital captive with a loss-prevention pilot. Start a private list of sellers of surplus gensets and switchgear from paused data center projects.

title: Solar Monitoring Data as Appliance Stethoscope
one_liner: Use the consumption data already sitting in installers' monitoring portals to spot dying air conditioners, resistance heat, hidden EVs and always-on pool pumps, then sell verified leads to HVAC and electrical contractors with a share back to the installer.
customer: HVAC and heat-pump contractors, EV-charger electricians and pool contractors pay per verified lead ($100-300). Installers earn a 20-30% revenue share. A later payer could be home-warranty companies and insurers who want early-failure signals.
problem: Post-2025, residential solar installers are short of revenue and sit on 500-5,000 past customers with monitoring already attached. HVAC contractors pay $150-500 per lead and spend most of their marketing budget in peak summer emergencies. Nobody mines the consumption stream (Enphase, SolarEdge and Tesla gateways record it every 5-15 minutes), where a failing compressor, a home heated by resistance strips or a new EV shows up clearly.
solution: Install-side product called Home Energy Plus. The installer emails past customers an opt-in for a free annual system checkup, connecting to their monitoring account through the OEM's API. An anomaly model flags: an AC drawing 25%+ more than on comparable weather days, short cycling, high winter baseline (resistance heat), overnight EV signature, pool pump running 24 hours. The customer gets a plain-language report ('your AC is likely low on refrigerant; a $99 tune-up now avoids a July failure'). Contractors bid for the lead in their service area, and the installer is paid a share. Homeowners can opt out at any time.
why_now: Federal 25C and 25D credits ended Dec 31, 2025, so heat-pump and HVAC contractors need intent-rich leads. Installers need recurring revenue from existing customers as new-install volume falls in 2026. OEM monitoring APIs are open to owner-authorized apps, and anomaly-detection models are cheap. Spring and fall shoulder seasons are when contractors most want planned replacements.
revenue_model: $100-300 per lead depending on trade and job size, split 70/30 with the installer. Optional $5-10 a month homeowner subscription for continuing reports. Later, sell early-failure signals to home-warranty companies at a per-home annual fee.
non_obvious_insight: An installer's monitoring portal is a stethoscope for the whole house, but installers use it only to answer why production is low. The consumption side is unlabeled and unused. Also, homeowners already trust the installer, and consent to share data is easiest to get from that relationship. A planned replacement in shoulder season is worth more to an HVAC company than an emergency job in July, because it fills idle crews.
first_30_days: Sign 3 installers with 1,000+ customers on Enphase or SolarEdge. Send the opt-in as a free annual checkup. Analyze 300 homes' historical data by hand and code up the first two signatures (AC and resistance heat). Produce 30 personalized reports. Sell the first 10 leads to two HVAC contractors at $150 each and measure close rate. Draft the consent and data-use terms with a privacy lawyer.

title: 48-Hour Patent Troll Response Desk for SMBs
one_liner: A flat-fee service that answers patent-troll demand letters within 48 hours with an AI-built claim chart, prior art, the assertion entity's litigation history and an attorney-signed response.
customer: Small e-commerce, restaurant-tech, app and SaaS companies (under about $20M revenue) receiving non-practicing-entity demand letters or complaints, plus IP insurers and trade associations that want a member benefit.
problem: Trolls price demands just below the cost of defense ($50k to $150k+), betting small targets will settle. Hourly-billing law firms can't respond cheaply, and the patent office's post-grant review path has gotten harder since 2025 with rising discretionary denials, though a March 2026 USPTO memo added small-business and domestic-manufacturing factors.
solution: 24-hour intake. LLM-assisted claim mapping of the patent to the target's product, a prior-art sweep, the patent's history (past invalidations, review petitions, family members, assignment chain), and the plaintiff's prior settlement pattern from court dockets. A partner patent attorney reviews and signs a response letter. Options: a shared 'campaign file' for other targets of the same troll, and an insured defense fund via membership.
why_now: Modern models can chart claims and search prior art in hours rather than billable weeks. Incumbent firms, paid by the hour, have little incentive to compress. The patent office's shifting policies make cheap district-court leverage more valuable.
revenue_model: Fixed $2.5k to $6k per response package, $99 to $299 monthly membership with pooled defense credits, and referral or insurance partnerships.
non_obvious_insight: The troll's model relies on low-cost, repeated assertion against many small targets, so it is undermined by a cheap, credible response and by a memory of it. Every response feeds a campaign file, and the second, third and hundredth target of the same entity get better and cheaper defense. That flips the network effect from the troll to the defenders, and word spreads fast that a target is not a soft settle.
first_30_days: Partner with one patent litigator on a flat-fee arrangement. Pull the top 20 active NPE campaigns from court dockets and pre-build claim-chart templates. Announce free 24-hour triage in small-business, Shopify and app-developer communities. Charge $3k for the first five full response packages.

title: Live Read-Aloud Rooms Staffed by Displaced Narrators
one_liner: Landline-friendly live group reading sessions led by professional audiobook narrators for isolated and low-vision elders, sold to agencies as a human alternative to free AI companion robots, with an attested 'human minutes' ledger.
customer: Area Agencies on Aging and state aging offices, senior-living operators, and Medicare Advantage or Medicaid plans buying social-isolation supplemental benefits. Families and libraries for the blind are a secondary channel.
problem: NY, FL and NJ now hand out ElliQ AI companions free, and 'loneliness reduction' is a funded policy goal, yet the buyer is buying synthetic contact. Meanwhile professional audiobook narrators are being squeezed by AI narration programs. Many isolated elders are on landlines, have low vision or fading attention, and cannot use apps or long-form video.
solution: Dial-in or smart-speaker reading rooms, 45 minutes each, 25-40 elders per room, with rooms by taste (mysteries, poetry, serialized novels, local history, faith). The narrator addresses listeners by name and takes requests. The platform logs attendance and issues a funder-facing 'verified live human minutes' report, which is the metric that a loneliness grant or plan benefit actually needs. Shared reading has a track record in dementia settings, so a memory-care track is included.
why_now: Governments are already in the market for loneliness tech and have discretionary budgets. AI narration has pushed skilled, warm voices into part-time work exactly as human-made is turning into a priced attribute. Older adults are adopting AI fast (23% of 65+ use ChatGPT), and a visible human alternative is a differentiator for buyers under pressure not to replace people with robots.
revenue_model: $35-45 per active elder per month, priced against ElliQ's $40 a month plus $250 upfront. Narrators earn about $45 per session, and a 30-person room yields roughly 40% gross margin. Contracts come from AAA and plan budgets on annual terms.
non_obvious_insight: The funder's real KPI is human contact minutes, not content. AI companions cannot honestly claim that ledger, but a narrator-led room can prove it. The scarce input is warm, trained voices, and AI has just made a pool of them cheap and underemployed.
first_30_days: Recruit 8 narrators from audiobook narrator communities and voice-actor unions. Run 3 free public rooms via a conference bridge and recruit elders through two county AAAs and a senior center. Collect attendance and self-reported loneliness scores and pitch the county AAA a $6-10k, three-month paid pilot.

title: Agentic Crypto Trace-and-Freeze Desk for Police
one_liner: An AI forensic analyst that traces a victim's stolen crypto across chains in minutes and drafts freeze requests, sold to local police who receive these reports but cannot trace.
customer: Police and sheriff's fraud and elder-crimes units, state AG consumer units, victim-service nonprofits and credit unions.
problem: Crypto-related complaints hit 181,565 and $11.4B in 2025, and victims report to local police who lack $20K+ blockchain forensics tools and training. Funds hop through swaps, bridges and exchange deposit addresses, and freeze windows are measured in hours.
solution: An officer or victim enters a transaction hash and an agent traces flows across major chains and bridges, clusters to exchange deposit addresses using open labels, and produces a freeze packet (evidence PDF and correctly formatted requests to exchange law-enforcement portals and stablecoin issuers). The officer approves, and recovery outcomes are tracked.
why_now: Tool-using agents can now run chain-analysis workflows and draft legal requests. Stablecoin issuers are cooperating on freezes at scale, and scam flows concentrate in a few tokens and exchanges.
revenue_model: $3-10K per agency per year, or about $150 per case, with elder-justice grant funding.
non_obvious_insight: The bottleneck in crypto recovery is procedural delivery, not analytics: which desk accepts what format, and how fast. An agent that sends the right request in minutes matters more than another dashboard.
first_30_days: Build tracing for USDT on Tron and Ethereum plus Bitcoin to the top 10 exchanges. Offer free traces to 10 sheriff's offices, track freezes, publish outcomes, and start $250 per month pilots with elder-justice grant funding lined up.

title: Meeting Subtext Captions for Neurodivergent Workers
one_liner: An on-screen coach for Zoom and Teams that flags conversational subtext (a question aimed at you, a topic shift, rising frustration) and supports post-meeting debriefs, sold through autism and ADHD coaches.
customer: Autism and ADHD coaching practices ($40-60 per client per month), employer neurodiversity hiring programs, and state vocational rehabilitation agencies.
problem: Autistic and ADHD adults often lose jobs and friendships over unspoken social subtext rather than skill. Human job coaches cost $75-150 an hour and cannot sit in every meeting. Loneliness among autistic adults is severe, and existing tools are scripts and courses that do not work in the live moment.
solution: A client-side app reading a live transcript and showing three private cue types ('direct question to you', 'time to wrap up', 'tone: irritated'), plus post-meeting debriefs shared with the coach and a rehearsal mode simulating hard meetings. Data stays local by default, and the coach dashboard shows patterns, not raw transcripts.
why_now: Real-time multimodal models now handle affect and conversational structure at low latency. Hybrid work makes meeting transcripts routine. Employers' neurodiversity hiring programs are maturing and need retention tools.
revenue_model: Per-seat license through coaching practices, employer accommodation budgets, and state vocational rehabilitation contracts.
non_obvious_insight: The right entry point is the coach's toolkit, not the consumer app. Coaches already have the trust, the payer relationship and the clinical framing, and AI extends their reach into moments they cannot attend.
first_30_days: Recruit 10 neurodiversity coaches through ADHD and autism coach networks. Pilot with 30 clients at $50 each, collect cue accuracy ratings and coach feedback, then approach two employers' neurodiversity leads.

title: Statutory Records-Portal Autopilot for Florida HOAs
one_liner: An email-in service that auto-posts a small Florida condo or HOA board's required documents to a compliant owner-only portal and tracks the deadlines.
customer: Self-managed Florida condo associations with 25+ units and HOAs with 100+ parcels, run by volunteer boards who cannot afford enterprise community-management software. The board treasurer or secretary pays, on the advice of the association's attorney or CPA.
problem: Florida law now requires these associations to post official records online. Condos of 25+ units must post the declaration and bylaws, minutes and meeting videos for the preceding 12 months, contracts and bid summaries over $500, budgets, financial reports, meeting notices and inspection reports and reserve studies, within 30 days of receiving or creating them (Fla. Stat. 718.111(12)(g)). HOAs with 100+ parcels had to post their equivalent documents behind an owner-only portal by January 1, 2025 (Fla. Stat. 720.303). Volunteer boards miss the posting clocks, and the resident-app market serves them poorly: a TownSq reviewer, a condo president, says the app gives 'no information that allows my board to manage our association effectively'. Others report that 'mailing settings were disabled... no one received mailed statements', a 2-page PDF shows only its first page, and requests cannot be edited after submission.
solution: Boards forward minutes, bids, contracts, budgets and inspection reports to a dedicated inbox, or drop meeting recordings into a folder. The system sorts each item into the statute's document categories and redacts protected information for board approval. It posts to an owner-only portal inside the 30-day clock and keeps meeting notices and agendas on their required schedule. It expires minutes and videos on a rolling 12-month cycle and keeps a compliance scorecard showing what is posted, what is missing and when each item is due. It also logs owner records requests with response deadlines.
why_now: The posting duties are in force: the HOA portal deadline was January 1, 2025, and the condo website provision is in the current statute. Florida has also been changing its condo and HOA rules, and attorneys are warning boards about compliance. A board that receives a records demand or a lawyer's letter will pay for a fix that week. The resident apps boards would otherwise use are rated poorly for board tasks.
revenue_model: $149-$299 per month per association depending on units, plus a $500 setup fee to load and classify the existing records. Referral fees to community-association attorneys and CPAs who recommend it. Add-ons: meeting-video hosting and a document translation for multilingual communities.
non_obvious_insight: The mandate creates a legal need in the segment with the least budget. Big vendors serve professionally managed communities, while the volunteer boards of small associations only need the documents posted correctly and on time. The statute itself says a failure to post 'is not in and of itself sufficient to invalidate any action or decision' of the board and specifies no fine, so the buyer is motivated by attorney advice, owner complaints and records-request risk, not by fines or features, and the pitch should reflect that. Evidence: the statute text at http://www.leg.state.fl.us/statutes/index.cfm?App_mode=Display_Statute&URL=0700-0799/0718/Sections/0718.111.html (condos) and http://www.leg.state.fl.us/statutes/index.cfm?App_mode=Display_Statute&URL=0700-0799/0720/Sections/0720.303.html (HOAs, Jan 1, 2025). Resident-app gaps from TownSq Community reviews (a condo president says it provides 'no information that allows my board to manage'; disabled mailed statements; a 2-page PDF shows only page 1) at https://itunes.apple.com/us/rss/customerreviews/id=945419466/sortby=mostrecent/xml. The pain is in board and owner communication, not the payments those apps focus on.
first_30_days: Days 1-10: build the inbox-to-portal flow for the 15 statutory document types and a redaction review screen. Have a Florida community-association attorney review the category list and the redaction rules. Days 10-20: run a free public compliance scan on 200 associations in Palm Beach, Broward and Miami-Dade using their public websites and email the board the gaps. Days 20-30: sign 2-3 community-association law firms as referral partners and take the first 10 associations at $199/month.

title: Pre-Engineered Single-Stair Plan Sets
one_liner: License stamped, fire-marshal-ready plan sets for 4-6 story single-stair buildings so small developers can use the new law without a $250K custom design.
customer: Small infill developers, church and nonprofit landowners and small architecture firms in single-stair states, plus modular fabricators.
problem: Seven states reformed single-stair rules in 2025 and Michigan followed in July 2026, promising about 10% cost savings, but architects and fire officials lack templates. Custom design is slow, local amendments add friction, and construction inputs are up 8.9% while multifamily starts fall.
solution: Engineered plan sets (4/5/6-story, 16-40 units, light-frame and mass-timber variants) with structure and MEP, a fire-safety compensation package, code narrative and a pre-meeting deck for local fire marshals. A network of local architects of record adapts them per site, and a per-state cost estimate is included.
why_now: New laws are taking effect (Michigan July 2026) and California AB 2074 awaits signature, while rising costs make small builders desperate for certainty.
revenue_model: $25-45K per plan license, $10-20K adaptation fee, referral fees from lenders and contractors, and a subscription for code updates.
non_obvious_insight: Legalization does not build housing; templates and fire-marshal comfort do. The first stamped precedent in each state becomes the local pattern, and plan sets have near-zero marginal cost.
first_30_days: Partner with a licensed architect who has single-stair experience. Draft one 4-story 16-unit set for Michigan. Presell three licenses to small developers at a $15K founder price and schedule a meeting with one fire marshal.

title: Battery-Aware 3PL for Military Drone Fleets
one_liner: A defense-cleared logistics provider built for lithium-powered drones: storage, battery conditioning, kitting, hazmat pack-out and repair depot for the Pentagon's tens of thousands of attritable UAS.
customer: Drone makers winning Drone Dominance and Gauntlet orders (many are 20-100 person startups) and the units and National Guard armories receiving drones. Pricing is per-drone kitting and per-pack conditioning fees plus storage and repair labor.
problem: The Drone Dominance Program targets more than 200,000 UAS by 2027, and about 60,000 will be ordered from Gauntlet 2 winners. Winners are startups that suddenly need to ship thousands of units per month. Lithium cells self-degrade, have Class 9 shipping rules and need storage-state management. Units have no facility to store, cycle and repair thousands of batteries, so drones sit in supply rooms until packs swell. Ammo-style logistics does not fit consumables that expire.
solution: A sprinklered, hazmat-capable facility near defense-drone clusters. Services include kitting (drone, packs, props, spares), pack-out to Class 9 rules, storage-state conditioning and cycling of packs, RMA and repair depot, serial and provenance tracking for NDAA-compliant chain of custody, and battery-safe return and disposal. Build toward CMMC-ready systems for controlled data.
why_now: Gauntlets 2, 2.5, 3 and 4 create recurring order waves every 6 months. New US drone tariffs took effect Sep 2026 and China's export controls on batteries and motors raise the value of domestic chain of custody. Amprius' $75M award shows domestic cells are ramping.
revenue_model: Per-kit handling ($15-40 per drone), storage per pallet-month, per-pack conditioning fees and repair-depot labor plus parts markup. Multi-year framework agreements with OEMs.
non_obvious_insight: A drone is only useful if its battery is at the right state of charge in the right hands within 30 days. The Pentagon is buying like it buys ammo, but there is no logistics operator designed for perishable lithium consumables. The bottleneck is the last 50 feet: the unit supply room.
first_30_days: Lease 10-15k sq ft of sprinklered flex space near a drone-OEM cluster. Get DOT hazmat training and a fire-protection review. Sign one Gauntlet 2 winner for a paid pilot of 1,000-2,000 kits with conditioning and RMA service.

title: Contingency-Fee Audit of OTA Markups and Payouts
one_liner: Mystery-shop every downstream reseller and reconcile every OTA payout, then take a share of the money and direct bookings recovered.
customer: Independent hotels of 20-200 rooms and small groups in Europe and the US paying 15-28% commissions.
problem: 51% of European hotels say OTAs sell below their loaded rate, up from 40% two years ago, and 26% do not know whether rates are passed on. Markups by Agoda, Citi, AA, Southwest and loyalty partners are invisible to rate-shopping tools. Hotels are paid after checkout, and commission, virtual-card fee and no-show errors go unchecked. In-house monitoring exists for chains (Radisson watches 1,600 properties), but independents have nothing.
solution: Combine automated and human shoppers that check rates across OTAs and reseller portals with screenshots per date, and reservation-level reconciliation of booked rate, commission, payout, card fees, cancellations and no-shows. Produce evidence packs to send to OTA account managers and a price-integrity dashboard that supports the case for direct booking.
why_now: Booking's payment service touched about 70% of its 2025 bookings, which concentrates the opacity. Google AI Overviews now reportedly show hotel prices and cut metasearch clicks, which pushes hotels to defend direct channels. Channel managers now expose reservation data.
revenue_model: 20-25% of recovered commission and no-show revenue, plus USD 99-299 per month for ongoing price-integrity monitoring.
non_obvious_insight: OTAs cannot audit themselves and hotels cannot see downstream markups, the same structural gap that made freight-bill and telecom-audit firms lucrative. The shopping evidence is the leverage in negotiations.
first_30_days: Offer 20 hotels a free 'leak report' covering 30 future dates, using human plus scripted shoppers. Convert the worst-leaking ones to contingency contracts, using hotel associations for introductions.

title: Moonlighting and IP Clearance for AI Experts
one_liner: A concierge that checks and files the employer-disclosure, IP-assignment and confidentiality paperwork professionals need before moonlighting as AI-training experts, and issues clean-provenance certificates that labs and vendors can rely on.
customer: Employed lawyers, bankers, doctors, consultants and engineers doing expert-data gigs pay $79-149 per clearance. Data vendors and lab legal or procurement teams pay for an annual B2B license.
problem: Millions of experts have signed up, many still employed at banks, law firms and hospitals with outside-activity approval rules (e.g. FINRA-registered staff), IP assignment and confidentiality duties. Some platforms even solicit prior work that former employers may own (HN Apr 2026). One trade-secret suit could freeze a vendor's programs, and workers risk termination or licence discipline.
solution: (1) A contract reader flags moonlighting, IP and confidentiality risk in the worker's agreement and handbook. (2) Templates for the employer disclosure or approval request. (3) A scanner for confidential markers in submitted work. (4) A 'clean-room certificate' per contributor. (5) An onboarding API vendors can require. A partner attorney covers the advice.
why_now: The Mercor breach and class actions have made vendor risk teams and lab counsel nervous. Reports of labs asking contractors for real past work samples raise provenance stakes. The scale of professionals moonlighting for AI companies is unprecedented.
revenue_model: Per-clearance fee for workers plus $50-250k annual vendor licences and per-contributor API fees.
non_obvious_insight: The buyer with money is the vendor's general counsel, not the worker, but the worker channel gives distribution and data. A database of moonlighting and IP policies for the top few thousand employers, built from worker submissions, becomes the moat.
first_30_days: Interview 20 moonlighting experts. Hand-build 50 employer-policy profiles (big banks, Big 4, large law firms, health systems). Run a manual $99 concierge clearance service. Pitch two mid-tier data vendors' compliance leads a paid pilot.

title: Insurer-Billable Circles for GLP-1 Quitters
one_liner: Twelve-week therapist-and-dietitian-led groups for people coming off GLP-1s, funded through behavioral-health and nutrition benefits rather than 'weight loss' budgets.
customer: Employers and carriers that just dropped GLP-1 coverage (about 14% more plan to by 2027) and the ex-users themselves ($299 cash cohorts to start). GLP-1 telehealth firms are a later channel, as a retention add-on.
problem: Only about a third of non-diabetic patients are still on therapy at 1 year, and cost is the top reason. Stoppers regain weight about 4x faster than behavioral losers, roughly 60% of ex-users intend to restart, and 70% report lost joy in eating. Returning food noise, binge eating and body-identity distress get no clinical owner, because pharma, PBMs and telehealth are paid for volume or price, not persistence.
solution: Small cohorts of about 8 are co-led by a licensed therapist (CBT/ACT, binge-eating experience) and a registered dietitian. Content covers returning food noise, structured eating, protein and resistance-training basics, and a relapse plan. A partner prescriber offers a taper or low-cost maintenance plan (for example a $149 pill) and defines restart triggers. Where clinically indicated (BED, adjustment disorder), sessions bill as in-network group psychotherapy (CPT 90853) with dietitian MNT, using honest coding only. Employers can instead buy it as a $450-700 per-participant 'transition benefit'.
why_now: Employer GLP-1 coverage for weight loss fell from 72% to 60% in 2026 and more employers are dropping it before open enrollment now. Brand pill prices fell to $149-$299 cash, so 'restart cheaply' is a real option. The Medicare $50 Bridge copay ends Dec 2027, and JAMA Psychiatry 2026 found GLP-1 use of about 50% among binge-eating-disorder patients.
revenue_model: In-network group-therapy and MNT claims, or an employer per-participant fee ($450-700 per 12-week cohort versus about $12k a year for the drug), plus an optional $29-49 per month prescriber maintenance subscription.
non_obvious_insight: Employers cut coverage to save money and created a pool of abrupt discontinuers with no plan. The only bundle in this space that insurers already pay for by law is behavioral-health group care, so the funding path is mental-health parity, not obesity medicine. That also aligns with the psychological cause of regain (food noise, identity, bingeing) rather than another diet.
first_30_days: Sign one therapist with binge-eating experience and one RD, both credentialed through an existing group practice. Recruit the first cohort of 8 from GLP-1 subreddits and Facebook groups at $299 cash. Approach three mid-size employers through brokers who have just announced dropped coverage. Track 12-week weight regain, binge episodes and restart rates against a naive expectation.

title: Cash-Flow Lifeline for K-12 Service Vendors
one_liner: Same-week invoice funding for small vendors who serve schools (after-school, tutoring, therapy, van companies), priced using each district's known payment calendar, with a service-continuity guarantee for principals.
customer: Small K-12 vendors paying a financing fee: after-school providers, contract speech, occupational and counseling practices, tutoring companies, small van and transportation contractors, and arts and PE providers. Principals are the sponsor and the free channel.
problem: Districts pay invoices 60 to 120 days late, and federal-grant reimbursements (21st Century, Title programs) lag further. Small vendors run out of cash and vanish in October, mid-year, leaving kids without services. Principals cannot legally pay faster and get blamed when the therapist stops coming. Generic factoring companies price district risk like a private customer or refuse it.
solution: Fund invoices within 48 hours at 90 percent advance. Verification is a text or QR 'services delivered' confirmation from the principal, which is the step district accounts payable needs anyway. Price risk using each district's board-approval calendar, warrant runs and reimbursement cycles, which we assemble from public board minutes. Add a continuity guarantee: if a funded vendor fails, a pre-vetted bench vendor steps in. Districts get a simple notice-of-assignment form to sign.
why_now: The July 2025 withholding of roughly $6.8B in federal education funds, released weeks later, showed how fragile the timing is. Post-ESSER budgets are tight, and small-business credit is harder for vendors with slow government customers. LLMs can now read board packets, purchase orders and approval calendars at scale to predict pay dates.
revenue_model: Fee of about 1.5 to 3 percent per invoice per 30 days advanced, plus a vendor subscription ($99 per month) for the delivery-confirmation and invoicing workflow.
non_obvious_insight: District default risk is near zero. The risk is timing, and timing is predictable if you know how boards and warrant runs work. The principal's confirmation, not the bank, is the bottleneck, so whoever owns that step owns the data. Investors dismiss K-12 as slow and poor, but the payer is a taxing authority, which is the safest receivable there is.
first_30_days: Recruit 10 small vendors from principals' and coordinators' contact lists, starting with after-school and therapy contractors that have already had payment problems. Raise $150k to $300k of angel or warehouse capital and fund the first invoices at a flat fee. Build the district payment calendars in a spreadsheet from public minutes, which becomes the pricing model and the data moat.

title: Passive Wellness Alerts From Water Meter Patterns
one_liner: A subscription that texts an adult child, or their parent's home-care agency, when an older person living alone has no expected water activity: no wearable, no camera, just the meter that is already on the house.
customer: Adult children of seniors who live alone ($12-19 per month). Home-care agencies and Area Agencies on Aging, which pay about $15-25 per client per month for a passive check on clients between visits. Later, Medicare Advantage plans offering supplemental benefits, at a per-member-per-month rate. Utilities are the channel partner, not the main payer.
problem: Roughly a quarter or more of Americans aged 65 and older live alone. Existing safety products get abandoned: pendants are left on the nightstand, wearables aren't charged, and cameras feel like surveillance and get unplugged. Families end up making anxious phone calls. Meanwhile the utility already has hour-level (or finer) consumption data from its smart meter, used only for bill disputes and leak alerts. Nobody has to wear or charge a meter.
solution: Learn each household's rhythm from interval water data: first use in the morning, number of daily events, typical overnight quiet. Alert on: no water event by the person's usual time plus a buffer, unusually long or repeated overnight use (possible wandering or confusion), continuous flow (leak or overflow), and sudden spikes. Escalate by text to a family member, then to a designated neighbor or a non-emergency wellness-check partner. Two data paths. Path A is a $40-bill-of-materials clamp-on or pulse reader on the customer's own meter, installed in 15 minutes by a caregiver, which needs no utility integration. Path B is a customer-consented feed from the utility's smart-meter system, with no hardware and utility co-branding. Leak protection is a free bonus that sells the same product to the utility.
why_now: The oldest baby boomers are now in their 80s, and 'Peak 65' has meant around 4 million Americans turning 65 every year through 2027. Home-care labor is scarce, so agencies need passive tools that extend a caregiver's reach. Smart-meter adoption among mid-size and large water utilities is now high, and those utilities are looking for customer-engagement wins after the billing complaints that followed rollouts. Green Button-style customer-directed data sharing exists for electricity but is almost absent for water. LLMs can also explain a pattern change in plain language to worried families.
revenue_model: Family subscription of $12-19 per month, plus optional hardware at cost or $49. B2B2C contracts with home-care agencies at $15-25 per client per month. Revenue share or flat fees from utilities per opted-in household. Later, Medicare Advantage supplemental-benefit contracts.
non_obvious_insight: Water use is the most honest sign of life in a house. Nobody can skip flushing for 36 hours, and it can't be faked, forgotten or unplugged. Japan's Zojirushi 'mimamori' kettle proved families will pay for a signal from an ordinary appliance. A utility meter is the same idea at the level of the whole house, and utilities are sitting on the data with no product.
first_30_days: Partner with two or three local home-care agencies and an Area Agency on Aging. Recruit 30 consenting seniors or families through caregiver support groups and Facebook groups for adult children. Install pulse or clamp-on readers on meters that support them, and run a 30-day baseline. Alert families by text and measure false-alarm and helpfulness rates. In parallel, approach one mid-size smart-meter utility with an opt-in pilot: consented data sharing at no cost, with the utility's logo on the program. Charge families $15 per month from day 31.

title: Investor-Cap Look-Through Checks for Title Companies
one_liner: An API that traces a buyer's LLC web to its parent and counts the homes it controls, so title and escrow can clear the ROAD Act's 350-home limit at closing.
customer: Title and escrow companies, closing attorneys and lenders in single-family-heavy metros. Secondary: mid-size investors (100-349 homes) who need to stay under the cap and prove it.
problem: The ROAD Act bars investors with more than 350 homes from buying existing houses. Compliance depends on affiliate holdings scattered across thousands of LLCs, which the closing agent cannot see. Large buyers will restructure into fragments, and mid-size investors suddenly need to manage headroom. Who is liable when a closing clears wrongly is unresolved.
solution: Entity resolution across county deed records, Secretary of State filings, registered-agent and address graphs and mailing addresses. It returns a portfolio count with a confidence score in seconds, an audit-ready evidence file for the closing, and a headroom dashboard for investors near the cap. Verify statute text, effective date, affiliate definition and exemptions first.
why_now: The law took effect in July 2026, and implementation questions are open now. Title agents are the natural chokepoint, as they already collect ownership details on entity purchases. Entity-resolution tooling and cheaper county record access make a small-team build feasible.
revenue_model: $15-40 per buyer-entity check. $500-2,000 per month SaaS for investors. Enterprise licenses to title underwriters.
non_obvious_insight: The people obligated to comply cannot compute the answer, and the people who can compute it are not in the transaction. The closing desk becomes the enforcement point, and mid-size investors treat their 350th home as a scarce budget, creating a second buyer for the same data.
first_30_days: Build for three metros where large single-family operators concentrate. Ingest deed and Secretary of State data. Sell paid pilots to 5 title agencies and 2 underwriters. Publish a free entity-count explainer to attract inbound.

title: ZIP-Level Appetite Radar for Distressed Markets
one_liner: A live map of which carriers are actually binding homes in which distressed ZIPs, sold to agents and to carriers owing coverage quotas.
customer: Independent agents and wholesale brokers in California (then Florida and Colorado). Carriers pay for pre-qualified submissions in ZIPs where they owe quota.
problem: The CA FAIR Plan hit 696,562 policies (up 8% since Sept 2025) and raised rates about 29.1%. Under the Sustainable Insurance Strategy, carriers get rate freedom in exchange for an 85% writing commitment in distressed ZIPs. Zurich, Mercury and CSAA say they are expanding, yet the June 2026 regulator release gave no numbers. Agents burn hours on declines, and nobody can see the ZIP-by-ZIP flip.
solution: Combine agent-contributed anonymized quote outcomes, licensed quote probing and rate/rule filing monitoring. Publish which carriers bind in each ZIP by roof age and mitigation class, with estimated savings versus FAIR. Agents get a 'who will write this' answer in seconds. Carriers pay a bounty per bound policy.
why_now: California's rewritten rulebook took effect in 2026 while regulator disclosure stayed opaque, so the information gap is largest now.
revenue_model: $99-249/month per agent, plus $75-200 carrier bounties per bound policy.
non_obvious_insight: Headlines say California is broken, but reality is a patchwork flipping ZIP by ZIP. Carriers with quota obligations are price-insensitive buyers of distribution, and agents are blind to them.
first_30_days: Recruit 20 independent agencies in wildfire-adjacent counties to a shared outcome log (a form and spreadsheet is enough). Publish a weekly 'who is writing' report and start charging at week four.
